title: Mohnish Pabrai's Q&A at the Value School (Madrid, Spain) on July 9, 2021
summary: A Q&A with Value School in Madrid covering why running a business makes one a better investor, how growing up in India gives comfort investing in chaotic markets like Turkey and China, and Pabrai's evolution from tech growth in the mid-90s to 20 years of Graham deep value and back toward Munger and Nick Sleep compounders. He details the Turkish holding bought at 4-5% of liquidation value, Rain Industries at a future PE of one, Prosus's holding discount, how to think about drawdowns without leverage, and Dakshana's plans.

ideas.idea: Having run a business is a huge edge for an investor because entrepreneurs manage three or four variables in their heads, not spreadsheets, and an investor must get to those same variables.
ideas.detail: Buffett: 'I'm a better investor because I'm a businessman and a better businessman because I'm an investor', and a thousand years of telling a fish about land is not worth one day walking on it. Projecting a trajectory through Excel is dangerous because nothing goes in a straight line.

ideas.idea: You cannot paint a country with one brush; within the chaos of emerging markets like India or Turkey there are great teams and businesses that transcend currency, inflation and leadership problems.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Growing up in India he saw well-organized operations like Coca-Cola inside the chaos, which gives him comfort diving into Turkey when friends dismiss it for its currency and leadership.

ideas.idea: Most of China is outside his circle of competence, but Alibaba and Tencent are understandable because they had Western investors early and are multinational in DNA despite being based in China.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Munger's view that the Chinese are natural capitalists trapped in a socialist system; capitalism there is still embryonic but developing quickly. He recently bought Alibaba.

ideas.idea: He has not abandoned deep value but added four or five knives to the Swiss army knife; he overdosed on Graham for 20 years and should have switched back to compounders around 2013-14.
ideas.detail: He was Buffett/Munger in the mid-90s, Graham for close to 20 years, and is now moving back toward Nick Sleep, Buffett and Munger. The best way to invest is a stake in a high-return-on-capital business with a long runway run by great management, even if you pay up. Most of the time compounders do best, but sometimes deep value wins, so stay flexible.

ideas.idea: Microsoft in early 2000 was a great business but a bad investment: over $600 billion market cap, under $10 billion cash flow, 60-70x earnings, and zero returns for 13-14 years despite huge revenue growth.
ideas.detail: Microsoft, GE and Cisco were the only three $600B+ companies; he told Microsoft employees holding 80-90% of their wealth in the stock that it looked like a bad investment. Even holding from 2000 to 2021 yielded only about 3x. Pabrai Funds was up over 70% in its first year (mid-1999 to mid-2000) by sidestepping the euphoria.

ideas.idea: Graham and Munger approaches use the same part of the brain: what does a dollar put out today return in five or ten years, via convergence to value or growth in value.
ideas.detail: In the Graham way you buy a $2 bill for a dollar and results depend on how long convergence takes; in the Munger way the dollar grows and results depend on the rate and duration. It is 'orgasmic' when the two worlds meet.

ideas.idea: His 2019 Turkish investment was bought at 4-5% of liquidation value ($20M market cap vs $500-600M liquidation value) with two great capital allocators, making it 'Nick Sleep on steroids'.
ideas.detail: He owns a third for about $7 million; the free float turned over every 15-17 days because Turkish investors trade for hours. In two years liquidation value rose to $800-900 million and market cap to over $100 million. The Sleep lesson: set it and forget it as long as the capital allocators are in place, even if the discount closes.

ideas.idea: Rain Industries, bought in 2015 at a 'future PE of one', went from a $200 million to over $2 billion market cap by 2018 when the expected earnings arrived.
ideas.detail: The company had close to $2 billion of revenue and he expected a year with $200 million of earnings within three or four years; not a cigar butt and not a great business, but a good business with a great capital allocator. He fell in love with the management.

ideas.idea: He is not a market timer; undervalued businesses exist at all times, only the geographies and industries change, so investing is a treasure hunt among 50,000 businesses.
ideas.detail: A company hitting a temporary air pocket gets taken out back and shot by the market, and that deserves attention. Ten-baggers are few and far between in any market.

ideas.idea: GameStop, AMC and Bitcoin are in bubble territory in 2021, but large US and Chinese tech are exceptional businesses that are merely not deeply discounted, not bubbles.
ideas.detail: Ron Insana's book TrendWatching shows bubbles exist all the time because humans vacillate between fear and greed. Being right about Bitcoin is irrelevant if you are neither long nor short; what matters is being right on what you own.

ideas.idea: 50% a year on small capital is possible with a dogged Graham approach and no more than three stocks, but it requires Buffett's intensity of going through every stock one at a time.
ideas.detail: Buffett went through the Moody's Manuals at least twice, looking for anomalies like a business earning $25 million trading for $15 million, and told a questioner to 'start with the A's'. Upanishad: your deepest desire is your destiny. Buffett's 1% outside Berkshire, often one stock, has compounded faster than Berkshire itself.

ideas.idea: With $20-30 million of capital he would put a quarter or a third of it into his best idea like the Turkish company; concentration is what makes small-capital returns meaningful.
ideas.detail: At his fund size the Turkish position could only be 4% of NAV because he could only invest $7 million.

ideas.idea: The Agnellis will hold Ferrari forever but Exor will move more capital out of mass-market autos over time, because Ferrari's 10,000 cars a year are worth more than Stellantis's millions.
ideas.detail: John Elkann is a learning machine and good capital allocator; the economics of Ferrari versus Stellantis are night and day. Pabrai's mistake was not holding Ferrari himself.

ideas.idea: Drawdowns are irrelevant if you have no leverage and know what your portfolio is worth rather than what the auction market prices it at every second.
ideas.detail: Munger's Berkshire lost more than half its value three times and it did not bother them. Any NYSE stock's yearly price range might be 50 to 100 while a home on Zillow moves 5-10%; auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot and that is what makes money. 'If wealth is lost, nothing is lost; if health is lost, something is lost; if character is lost, everything is lost.'

ideas.idea: Holding company discounts like Prosus/Naspers are very common; the market pays less when a Picasso and a Matisse are shoved down its throat together.
ideas.detail: Koos Bekker's analogy from a Naspers call: roughly $200 billion of Tencent stock plus $40 billion of other investments trading at maybe under $150 billion. Sometimes the market gives you things on a platter.

ideas.idea: Traits that make a great investor can be at odds with those that make a great marriage, and Buffett's singular focus was compensated for by his wife Susie until she left in the 1970s.
ideas.detail: Buffett worked from an office off his bedroom from 7 AM to 10 PM engrossed in the Moody's Manual; Peter Buffett said his dad would not throw baseballs but was home for dinner every day. With the right partner it can work.

ideas.idea: Munger is far more well-rounded than Buffett: investing is just one interest alongside designing dormitories, boats and caravans, and he does not obsess over his annualized compounding rate.
ideas.detail: Most of what Pabrai learned from Munger came from observing him with friends, family and grandkids rather than from anything Munger said.

ideas.idea: Dakshana is exploring a joint venture to train high-school graduates for two years in software engineering and entrepreneurship, cutting four years off the current path through university.
ideas.detail: Universities are bloated aircraft carriers; if the new model works he is willing to abandon the existing one. Philanthropy needs head as well as heart: measure money in against good to society out, and be willing to fail.
